notes: Deep dorsal horn parvalbumin+ glycinergic interneurons (dPVs) receive convergent proprioceptive and cutaneous input from the paw and provide divergent ipsilateral inhibition to ventral horn pre-motor and motor networks, controlling the timing and magnitude of cutaneous-evoked flexor and extensor muscle activity. Descending neuromodulation mimicked by 5-HT, dopamine, and NMDA amplifies dPV output while sensory input shapes its temporal dynamics, and manipulating dPVs during treadmill locomotion alters limb kinematics at the stance-to-swing transition and step-cycle timing at higher speeds, implicating sensory convergence plus inhibitory divergence in smooth, context-appropriate phase transitions.
animal_study: Test state dependence of the convergent sensory gating by recording dPV responses before and after monoamine application during locomotion, and by selectively activating or silencing dPVs at specific step-cycle phases to measure changes in cutaneous-evoked reflex timing and stance-to-swing kinematics.
robot_sim: Implement a dPV-analog inhibitory population receiving convergent proprioceptive and cutaneous inputs and providing divergent ipsilateral inhibition to MN and premotor pools, with a descending-modulation gain; ablate it to test its effect on stance-to-swing transition timing and cutaneous reflex gating.
flags: Abstract never names the species (intersectional genetics and parvalbumin labeling suggest mouse) so animals is left empty per the grounding rule; the dPV pathway (convergent cutaneous/proprioceptive inhibitory gating via dorsal horn interneurons) may also deserve its own feedback vocabulary entry beyond 'Cutaneous stance modification'.

notes: In intact humans, short-latency non-reciprocal group I inhibition from the medial gastrocnemius nerve onto the conditioned soleus H-reflex, disynaptic and present at rest in most subjects, is significantly reduced during treadmill walking, with some subjects showing significant excitation, mirroring the reduction of resting Ib inhibition toward excitation seen in walking cats. The reduction may be partially accounted for by activation of the triceps surae itself.
animal_study: Replicate with intracellular recording in an animal model: measure short-latency group I inhibition in ankle extensor motoneurons at rest, during matched isometric activation, and during locomotion, to separate walking-related from load-related suppression of the Ib pathway.
robot_sim: Implement disynaptic Ib inhibition onto ankle extensors with a locomotor-phase-dependent gain reduction (partial reversal toward excitation during gait); ablate the phase switch to test its effect on stance extensor activity.

notes: In freely walking cats with the medial gastrocnemius functionally isolated, changes in ankle extensor activity across walking conditions correlate strongly with Ib (force) afferent activity rather than with Ia or group II activity, and force feedback contributes about 30% of total muscle activity during level walking. The pathway gain from muscle force to motoneuron depolarization is length-independent while loop gain rises with length through the intrinsic force-length property, and force feedback's contribution increases during upslope and decreases during downslope walking, providing a simple mechanism for compensating terrain changes.
animal_study: Extend the isolated-muscle sloped-walking protocol with underfoot force perturbations (dropping or lifting the peg underfoot) to other limb levels or species, estimating force-feedback gain and its share of stance muscle activity across terrain.
robot_sim: Implement autogenic Ib force feedback on the ankle extensor with length-dependent loop gain (via the force-length property) supplying roughly 30% of stance activation; ablate it during slope changes to test terrain compensation.

notes: In supported stepping of human infants, hip flexion combined with high limb load prolongs stance and delays swing, whereas hip extension with low load shortens stance and advances swing, remarkably similar to reduced cat preparations. Hip position and load show an inverse relationship at the time of swing initiation, indicating the two sensory factors combine to regulate the stance-to-swing transition, consistent with similar brainstem and spinal walking circuitry in infants and cats.
animal_study: In a spinal or decerebrate cat preparation, independently manipulate hip joint angle and extensor load during treadmill stance to map the interaction surface controlling swing initiation, directly testing the inverse hip-position/load relationship found in infants.
robot_sim: Implement swing-initiation gating as a combined hip-extension and low-load condition with an inverse interaction between hip angle and limb load; ablate either input to reproduce prolonged stance and delayed swing.
flags: Abstract does not type the afferents behind the hip-position and load regulation of swing initiation (in the vocabulary this would map to 'Ia or II stance to swing' plus a load/Ib-type gate) so feedback is left empty per the grounding rule.

notes: A half-center CPG model with a slowly inactivating persistent sodium current reproduces the phase-dependent effects of brief afferent stimulation on fictive locomotion in cats, in which stimulation can shorten or prolong the current locomotor phase and reset the cycle depending on stimulation phase and nerve. Dynamic-systems analysis of the model identifies the mechanisms of locomotor rhythm resetting, supporting phase-dependent afferent access to the CPG as the substrate for sensory correction of the locomotor rhythm.
animal_study: Apply brief nerve stimuli at systematically varied phases of fictive locomotion in immobilized animals and compare the measured phase-response curves (phase shortening or prolongation, cycle resetting) against the half-center model's predictions.
robot_sim: Implement the persistent-sodium half-center CPG and apply brief phase-tagged stimuli to reproduce the cat phase-response behavior (phase-dependent shortening, prolongation, and resetting); use the model's dynamic-systems structure to analyze the resetting mechanisms.

notes: Review of automated parameter optimization for computational neuron models, distinguishing feature-based, point-by-point voltage-trace, and multi-objective error functions, and detailing search algorithms including brute force, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, evolution strategies, differential evolution, and particle-swarm optimization; the Neurofitter package combines a phase-plane trajectory density fitness function with several of these searches, replacing intractable hand tuning as model complexity grows.
robot_sim: Adopt automated multi-objective optimization (feature-based or trace-based fitness with evolutionary or annealing search) for tuning CPG and reflex-model parameters instead of hand tuning, per the reviewed error-function and search-algorithm taxonomy.

notes: Parameterizes noise-driven Lotka-Volterra stable heteroclinic channel (SHC) cycles so that each saddle's mean sub-period can be designed independently (analytic approximation within 2%), with the noise magnitude setting the mean period to near integration-step accuracy. The architecture gives pattern generators immediate multisensory responsiveness by modulating dwell time at a phase of oscillation, applicable to robot control and to modeling context-dependent behaviors with rapid, input-precipitated transitions in frequency and phase.
animal_study: Test the SHC dwell-time prediction in a locomoting animal: deliver brief multisensory perturbations at known phases of the cycle and quantify phase-specific changes in dwell time and cycle period as the model predicts.
robot_sim: Implement a Lotka-Volterra SHC-cycle pattern generator with per-saddle dwell-time design and noise-set mean period; deliver multisensory perturbations to test immediate phase responsiveness against a half-center CPG.

notes: Drosophibot, a hexapod robot and dynamic simulation of Drosophila melanogaster, captures fruit-fly biomechanics through dynamically scaled joint elasticity and movement speed, a biomimetic actuator scheme converting neural activity into motion as in insects, proprioception from all leg joints and strain sensing from all leg segments, and passively compliant tarsi. Its actuators and sensors are shown to perform in an animal-like way, providing a testbed in which an insect neural walking controller can be evaluated in simulation and transferred to hardware.
animal_study: Record leg-joint proprioceptor and leg-segment strain-organ activity in walking flies to validate the biomimetic sensing assumptions (scaled joint elasticity, per-segment strain sensing) implemented in Drosophibot.
robot_sim: Replicate Drosophibot-style biomimetic sensing (per-joint proprioception, per-segment strain feedback) and neural-activity-to-motion actuation in simulation; ablate the strain-sensing channel to quantify its role in the insect neural walking controller.

notes: Argues, on the stick insect walking system, that continuous dynamic models in the form of differential equations outperform discontinuous bistable descriptions of coordinated locomotion: they permit inclusion of biological detail, suitability for simulation, and, most importantly, parameter manipulation to make predictions about system behavior in a system where coordination emerges from concerted joint dynamics interacting across dynamical scales.
animal_study: Use the continuous models' parameter manipulations to design stick-insect walking perturbation experiments (for example altered joint loading), whose predicted kinematic outcomes can then be tested experimentally.
robot_sim: Build the stick-insect walking system as continuous differential-equation joint models, using parameter manipulation to predict coordination changes and comparing against discontinuous bistable alternatives.

notes: The abstract attached to this record describes the brain's default mode network rather than motor control, an apparent database mismatch, so no content can be grounded from it and the content fields are left empty; the record needs its abstract re-sourced from the DOI before curation.
flags: ABSTRACT MISMATCH: the queue's abstract is default-mode-network text, not Pearson's motor-control review; all content fields left empty per the grounding rule. Re-fetch the abstract from DOI 10.1146/annurev.ne.16.030193.001405 and re-curate. is_review was inferred from the Annual Reviews title/venue only.

notes: A three-neuron network reconstructed in culture generates the respiratory rhythm of the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis, with postinhibitory rebound excitation identified as the mechanism important for rhythm generation, establishing an in vitro model system in which the neural basis of rhythm generation can be studied at the level of identified cells.
animal_study: Reconstruct and pharmacologically manipulate the identified three-neuron ensemble in culture (for example blocking postinhibitory rebound) to test the causal sufficiency of rebound excitation for rhythm generation; analogous ablations are possible in other identified invertebrate CPGs.
robot_sim: Implement a three-neuron CPG relying on postinhibitory rebound excitation for rhythm generation; ablate the rebound mechanism to test rhythm loss and compare its burst-termination dynamics with adaptation-based half-centers.
flags: The animal (pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis) has no exact name in the animals vocabulary, so animals is left empty; propose adding 'Mollusk' or 'Snail' if non-arthropod invertebrate CPGs should be captured.

notes: In rhythmic leg movements of human infants, load-related feedback prolongs whichever phase is more loaded: stepping on a treadmill, kicking against a plate, and kicking in sitting lengthen extension, whereas air-stepping with ankle weights lengthens flexion, and infants exerting lower forces show shorter extensor durations. Manipulating weight-bearing during stepping confirms the effect, showing that the degree of loading directly and incrementally affects the duration of the loaded phase.
animal_study: In animal rhythmic-movement preparations (for example spinal air-stepping versus supported stance), manipulate limb loading with weights or foot-plate contact to test whether the more loaded phase lengthens in a graded manner as in infants.
robot_sim: Implement load-dependent phase-duration modulation, in which the more loaded phase of the step cycle lengthens incrementally, in a stepping network; ablate the load input to test phase-duration changes.
flags: The load-related feedback that prolongs the loaded phase is not typed to an afferent class in the abstract (an Ib-family pathway by mechanism) so feedback is left empty per the grounding rule.

notes: In cadaveric hips under functional load, each capsular ligament (iliofemoral medial and lateral arms, pubofemoral, ischiofemoral) acts as the primary rotational restraint somewhere within the full range of motion, the ligamentum teres acts as a secondary restraint in high flexion, adduction and external rotation, and the iliofemoral lateral arm and ischiofemoral ligaments are primary restraints in about two-thirds of the positions tested, quantifying the passive soft-tissue contribution to hip rotational stability.
robot_sim: Use the measured capsular-ligament restraint contributions as position-dependent passive hip rotational stiffness and limits in musculoskeletal or robotic models of the lower limb.
flags: Orthopaedic cadaver-biomechanics study, not a sensory-afferent paper; relevant to SADb only as passive hip rotational-restraint data for biomechanical models, so Ben should decide on retention.

notes: Human infants who sustain forward stepping can also step sideways and backward on a treadmill, with the same relationships of stance and swing phase durations to cycle duration across directions and speeds, and no discrete changes in electromyographic or temporal parameters when direction is varied continuously, supporting a single locomotor CPG controlling different walking directions with direction-specific muscle tuning (for example hamstrings much more active in backward swing).
animal_study: In animal models, rotate the walking direction gradually on a treadmill while recording limb kinematics and EMG, testing for continuous retuning rather than discrete pattern switching as evidence for a shared CPG.
robot_sim: Drive a single locomotor CPG through a direction-dependent motoneuron mapping and test continuous direction changes for graded, EMG-like retuning without discrete pattern switches.

notes: In cats during quadrupedal locomotion, staggered thoracic lateral hemisections largely spare short-, mid- and long-latency homonymous and crossed forelimb reflexes from superficial radial nerve stimulation together with their phase modulation, but significantly reduce or abolish mid- and long-latency homolateral and diagonal responses in hindlimb muscles. This shows a considerable loss of cutaneous reflex transmission from cervical to lumbar levels after incomplete spinal cord injury despite preserved phase modulation, likely impairing coordinated responses to external perturbations across the four limbs.
animal_study: Combine staggered hemisections with targeted restoration of cervico-lumbar transmission (for example stimulation-based approaches) and quantify recovery of homolateral and diagonal cutaneous reflex responses and of forelimb-hindlimb coordination during locomotion.
robot_sim: Model phase-gated cutaneous reflex pathways with interlimb homolateral and diagonal projections onto all four limbs; ablate the cervico-lumbar links to reproduce the loss of hindlimb responses and weakened interlimb coordination after incomplete spinal cord injury.
flags: Forelimb-to-hindlimb cutaneous interlimb reflex reorganization (homolateral/diagonal responses after incomplete SCI) fits no existing feedback vocabulary entry, so feedback is left empty; propose a 'Cutaneous interlimb reflex' term if Ben wants this family captured.

notes: Horizontal-plane rigid-body models with pairs of virtual elastic legs in intermittent ground contact exhibit periodic gaits whose stability is largely determined by geometrical criteria, showing that mechanics alone can confer asymptotic stability in heading and body orientation without neural feedback, motivating application to rapidly running cockroaches in the companion paper.
animal_study: Perturb heading and body orientation of rapidly running insects and test whether recovery is achieved passively, without corrective changes in neural timing, consistent with mechanically conferred asymptotic stability.
robot_sim: Implement the horizontal-plane passive compliant-legged dynamics with intermittent foot contact in a legged-robot model and test whether heading and orientation stability emerge from mechanics alone before adding any neural feedback (preflex behavior).

notes: In human radial-nerve recordings from finger extensor muscles, three discrete and statistically pairwise-independent response markers, the initial burst at stretch onset, the deceleration response at the start of hold, and prompt silencing during imposed shortening, discriminate muscle spindle primaries from secondaries (the dynamic index alone is a poor discriminator with a unimodal distribution), while Golgi tendon organ afferents give negligible stretch responses; the battery supports a probability-based classification of human muscle afferents.
animal_study: Apply the three-marker classification battery with ramp-and-hold and superimposed sinusoidal stretches to muscle afferents in other human muscles or in animal preparations, building the probability-based classification database the paper proposes.
robot_sim: Implement Ia and II spindle models that reproduce the discrete dynamic markers (initial burst, deceleration response, silence during shortening) and validate the model's response statistics against these human single-unit data.

notes: In decerebrate cats, plantaris nerve group I stimulation evokes short-latency disynaptic IPSPs in medial gastrocnemius motoneurons at rest but EPSPs during the extensor phase of MLR-evoked fictive locomotion, also elicited by selective group Ia activation via Achilles tendon stretch, indicating an excitatory group Ia and Ib feedback system that reinforces ongoing extensor activity during stance. In clonidine-treated spinal preparations the resting inhibition disappears without appearing as excitation, suggesting locomotion inhibits the inhibitory interneurons operating at rest.
animal_study: Record group I-evoked PSPs intracellularly in ankle extensor motoneurons throughout the fictive step cycle in different preparations (MLR-evoked versus spinal with clonidine) to dissociate suppression of the resting inhibitory pathway from expression of disynaptic excitation.
robot_sim: Implement phase-switched group I pathways onto synergist ankle extensor motoneurons, disynaptic inhibition at rest and disynaptic excitation during the extensor phase; ablate the switch to test reinforcement of extensor activity during stance.
flags: Group Ia disynaptic excitation of synergists during extension (tendon-stretch-evoked EPSPs) has no vocabulary entry; 'Ib disynaptic excitation' is used for the Ib component, and an 'Ia disynaptic excitation' term is proposed if Ben wants the Ia component captured.

notes: The two standard spike-frequency adaptation mechanisms have distinct effects on synchronization of excitatorily coupled neurons: M-current adaptation alters the mechanism of repetitive firing, whereas calcium-dependent afterhyperpolarization adaptation works by shunting incoming synapses, a mechanism that also applies in networks with recurrent inhibition. A two-variable reduced model arising near certain bifurcations and a derived one-dimensional map capture the shunting behavior.
animal_study: Pharmacologically separate the two adaptation mechanisms in coupled neural populations (selective blockers of the slow voltage-dependent potassium current versus the calcium-dependent current) and test the predicted opposite effects on synchronization.
robot_sim: Implement both adaptation types (AHP-like synaptic shunting versus M-current-like alteration of the firing mechanism) in coupled CPG oscillators and compare their effects on synchronization and burst termination.

notes: Chronic spinal kittens on a split-belt treadmill maintain a common hindlimb rhythm across two- to threefold belt speed differences by prolonging the flexion or first extension phase of the fast-belt limb and shortening the flexion phase of the slow-belt limb, with extreme differences producing 2, 3, or even 4 fast-limb steps per slow-limb cycle; support-phase duration mainly follows each limb's own belt speed. All phases of the step cycle are thus modifiable, with several spinal mechanisms coordinating the limbs.
animal_study: Run chronic spinal animals on split-belt treadmills with graded belt speed differences and record hindlimb EMG to map the limits of rhythm sharing and the rules of per-limb phase modification across preparations.
robot_sim: Implement spinal interlimb coordination with per-limb phase modification under asymmetric timing commands (a split-belt analog), including shared rhythm up to two- to threefold speed differences and integer multiple stepping beyond that.

notes: During MLR-evoked fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, Renshaw cells discharge rhythmically in phase with the motoneuron pools that excite them, with extensor Renshaw activity peaking at the end of extension coincident with extensor motoneuron hyperpolarization; Renshaw inhibition of quadriceps Ia inhibitory interneurons is not sufficient to disrupt the phasing of reciprocal inhibition, though extensor Renshaw cells may contribute to the late-extension decline in IaIN discharge. Ia reciprocal IPSPs in motoneurons vary significantly in amplitude across the fictive step cycle.
animal_study: Record Renshaw cells, Ia inhibitory interneurons, and alpha-motoneurons simultaneously during fictive locomotion, and test the Renshaw-to-IaIN contribution at end-extension by selectively stimulating or silencing Renshaw cells through the step cycle.
robot_sim: Implement Renshaw cells phase-locked to motoneuron pools with recurrent inhibition onto Ia inhibitory interneurons; ablate the Renshaw-to-IaIN connection to test the late-extension decline of reciprocal inhibition.
flags: The queue abstract is truncated mid-sentence at its end ('...in which the motoneuron was most'); curation deliberately excludes the cut-off clause.

notes: In cat soleus muscle spindle primary endings under sinusoidal stretch, combined static and dynamic fusimotor stimulation is dominated by static action at small amplitudes (up to about 50 micrometers) with the dynamic contribution growing progressively with stretch amplitude; at response peaks the two actions sum (dynamic stronger), whereas in troughs static action occludes the weaker dynamic action, and phase differences between conditions remain below 20 degrees. The findings characterize how fusimotor set shapes Ia encoding of stretch.
animal_study: Stimulate pairs of static and dynamic fusimotor fibers during controlled sinusoidal stretching in other muscles or species to test the generality of the amplitude-dependent summation and occlusion rules for spindle primary endings.
robot_sim: Implement spindle-primary afferent encoding with separate static and dynamic fusimotor drives reproducing the amplitude-dependent summation and occlusion behavior, and modulate fusimotor set during locomotion to shape Ia feedback.

notes: Review of propriospinal interneurons as short- and long-distance relays within the spinal cord that link motor circuits controlling muscles across the forelimbs, trunk, and hindlimbs; their coordinating role in the intact cord, and the formation and activation of circuits established by spared propriospinal interneurons, may promote the re-emergence of locomotion after spinal cord injury disrupts descending commands, with supporting progress in animal models and human patients.
animal_study: In spinal cord injury animal models, test whether activating spared propriospinal circuits (through training or stimulation) re-establishes forelimb-hindlimb locomotor coupling as the review proposes.
robot_sim: Implement short- and long-propriospinal intersegmental coupling between locomotor circuits for the limbs and trunk; ablate the coupling to emulate spinal-cord-injury disconnection and test recovery through its re-activation.
flags: The abstract references unspecified 'animal models of SCI' without naming species, so only Human is listed; add the relevant species after checking the full text.

notes: In neonatal rodent spinal cord, removing extracellular calcium unmasks bursting in about 75% of interneurons in the locomotor CPG area with a concomitantly upregulated persistent sodium current, and putative CPG interneurons including commissural and Hb9 interneurons express riluzole-sensitive I(NaP)-dependent bursting, with most bursting cells showing pacemaker-like frequency increases under depolarization. Upregulating I(NaP) with veratridine induces riluzole-sensitive bursting and slows the locomotor rhythm, establishing I(NaP) pacemaker properties as generators and frequency regulators of the locomotor rhythm.
animal_study: Apply I(NaP) blockers (riluzole) and enhancers (veratridine) to isolated spinal cord preparations while recording locomotor-like activity, testing the predicted slowing or loss of the rhythm with I(NaP) reduction and speeding with enhancement.
robot_sim: Add persistent-sodium pacemaker currents to CPG interneurons and modulate the I(NaP) conductance (model analogs of riluzole and veratridine) to test rhythm initiation, frequency regulation, and burst termination.
flags: Species is given only as 'neonatal rodents', listed here under 'Mammals'; narrow to Rat or Mice from the full text if the exact species matters.

notes: Review arguing that vertebrate locomotion emerges from distributed control, spinal CPGs as coupled-oscillator feedforward controllers plus multiple reflex feedback loops, activated and modulated by descending pathways, whose relative contributions vary among animals with body size, intrinsic mechanical stability, time to reach locomotor maturity, and speed. It hypothesizes that distal joints rely more on feedback control than proximal joints, and positions robots and neuromechanical simulations as complements to experiments through what-if scenario testing.
animal_study: Test the distal-versus-proximal feedback hypothesis by locally perturbing or denervating feedback at individual joints of locomoting animals and comparing the compensation achieved at distal versus proximal joints.
robot_sim: Build hybrid CPG-plus-reflex architectures with joint-dependent feedback weighting (stronger feedback at distal joints) and use what-if simulations to test the proposed division of labor across body size, intrinsic mechanical stability, and speed.
